title: Instances
blurb: Virtual machines. What was asked for is the spec; what the node reports is the status, and they are shown together.
empty: Nothing runs in this project yet. An instance is a virtual machine: an image to boot, a size, and a network it can be reached on.

fields.label: Flavor
fields.help: A named size from the cell's menu. Picking one sets the vCPUs, memory and root disk below; typing sizes instead needs the project's leave.

fields.label: Image family
fields.help: A family is a name for a line of builds — `debian-13`, not one digest. It resolves to the newest image in it at the moment this instance is created, and the instance keeps that image for life: a family publishing a new build never changes what is already running.

fields.label: Root disk
fields.help: Set by the flavor when one is picked.

fields.label: Power
fields.help: What it should be doing. Asking twice is the same as asking once.

fields.label: Ports
fields.whenEmpty: This project has no ports yet, and does not need any: name a network above and one is made. A port of your own is for the case where the address has to outlive the machine.
fields.help: For a NIC that already exists — one holding an address you want this instance to keep. To simply put a machine on a network, name the network above and the port is made for you.

fields.label: Extra disks
fields.whenEmpty: This project has no volumes yet. Make one under Volumes and it can be attached here — the attachment itself is made for you.
fields.help: Attached once the instance is on a node. Take one off the list to detach it.

fields.label: Networks
fields.help: Left empty, this instance joins your project's default network — made the first time somebody needs it, so two machines in a project can talk without anybody configuring anything.

fields.label: SSH keys
fields.help: Read by cloud-init inside the instance on its **first** boot and never again, so adding one to a machine that has already started does nothing to that machine. Without a key and without a password set in user-data, the console is the only way in.

fields.label: User data
fields.help: Handed to the instance on first boot.

fields.label: Pinned to node
fields.help: Left empty the scheduler chooses. Moving it afterwards is a migration, not an edit.

fields.label: Anti-affinity group
fields.help: Instances in one group are kept off the same node — what keeps a service alive when a machine dies.

fields.label: Keeping them apart is
fields.help: A rule refuses a node that already runs a member — three replicas of a database must not share a machine even if that means one stays down. A wish takes a crowded node over not running at all, which is what twelve web servers want.

fields.label: Affinity group
fields.help: The opposite ask: instances in one group are placed together. For a pair that talks constantly — an application and the cache it reads on every request — where a hop between machines is the whole latency budget.

fields.label: Keeping them together is
fields.help: A rule refuses every node but the one the group is already on, and says which that is. A wish places elsewhere rather than not at all.

fields.label: Required node labels
fields.help: Only nodes carrying all of these.

fields.label: Start order
fields.help: Lower starts first; the same number is a group that starts together. Matters after a power cut, when a node brings back everything it holds at once and the database loses the race for disk to a dozen web servers.

fields.label: Let the group ahead settle
fields.help: Measured from the newest start in that group, not each member in turn — a hundred instances at thirty seconds each would be fifty minutes of nothing happening.

fields.label: If its node stops answering
fields.help: Only for an instance whose storage every node can reach. One on local storage that is started elsewhere is an empty machine wearing a familiar name. Nothing is moved until the node has been quiet long enough that its own agent has certainly stopped what it was running — a node with no fencing deadline is never recovered from.

fields.label: Show console output
fields.help: Publishes what the operating system inside writes to its serial console, so it can be read here. Off by default because it costs a report every time it logs a line. An instance that is not running shows its last output whether this is on or not.

fields.label: Passed-through devices
fields.help: A class, not a machine's address. Two of the same class means two devices. An instance holding one cannot be live-migrated — a device's state is in hardware and cannot be transferred.

fields.label: Minimum CPU level
fields.help: What the image needs to run. RHEL 9 and CentOS Stream 9 need x86-64-v2 or they will not boot.

agreements.label: Power
agreements.note: The node has not brought the instance to the state that was asked for. Its Ready condition says why.

agreements.label: Node
agreements.note: The scheduler has picked a node the reporting agent is not; a migration is in flight, or the pin was changed under a running instance.

title: Volumes
blurb: Block devices. A volume knows nothing about who has it open — that is an attachment.
empty: No disks yet. A volume is storage of its own — attach it to an instance, detach it, and it is still there when that instance is thrown away.

fields.label: Pool
fields.help: Left empty, the cell chooses: the accepting pool with the most room. Naming one is for operators pinning a volume to specific hardware — a tenant cannot list pools and does not need to.

fields.label: From image
fields.help: Left empty the volume comes up blank.

fields.label: From snapshot
fields.help: Restores that snapshot into a new volume. A volume is never restored in place, so this is what restoring means.

fields.label: From backup
fields.whenEmpty: This project has no backups yet. A backup is made from a volume, or on a schedule.
fields.help: Restores that copy into a new volume. This is the way back when the pool the volume lived on is gone.

fields.label: Encryption key
fields.help: Not yet: this cell has no key manager, so a key here is refused and the bytes are stored in the clear. The field is here for when one exists.

fields.label: IOPS
fields.help: What this volume may take. Left empty — which is stored as a zero — it takes the pool's ceiling, if the pool has one, and asking for more than the ceiling gets the ceiling rather than a refusal.

fields.label: Read
fields.help: Read bandwidth. Left empty it takes the pool's ceiling, if the pool has one.

fields.label: Write
fields.help: Write bandwidth. Left empty it takes the pool's ceiling. Separate from reads because they are not the same cost on any backend here: a write to a replicated Ceph pool is three writes.

agreements.label: Size
agreements.note: The pool has not finished growing the device to the size that was asked for.

title: Attachments
blurb: Attaching is its own object, so a crash mid-way leaves a truthful record rather than a volume nobody can reattach.

fields.label: Node
fields.help: Where the volume will be opened. Taken from the instance.

agreements.label: Node
agreements.note: The node that was asked to open it is not the node that reported. Nothing is attached until they agree.

title: Networks
blurb: A private network of this project's own. Instances on one reach each other wherever they are placed, and nothing outside the project can join. Its VNI is the tag this cell puts on the network's packets to keep them apart from every other network's on the same wire.
empty: No networks of your own yet. One is made for you the first time an instance needs somewhere to be; make one here to decide the addresses yourself.

fields.label: On the machine's own wire
fields.help: A bridge that already exists on the nodes — `br0`, `vmbr0`. Instances on this network go straight onto whatever the machine is on: the house LAN, a VLAN, a lab network. Their addresses come from whatever serves that wire and this platform allocates none, holds no gateway and enforces no security group. Empty is the ordinary case. Only a cell operator may set it — it is a decision about the machine, not about a project.

fields.label: Carries real addresses
fields.help: The prefixes on this network's subnets are routed to this cell by whoever is above it, so an address from one is an address the world can reach. Only a cell operator may say so — a tenant who could would mint themselves a public range by typing a CIDR.

fields.label: Addresses announced by
fields.help: What this cell does by default for addresses from this network. An individual address may say otherwise. Meaningless on a network that carries no real addresses.

fields.label: MTU
fields.help: 1450 when left empty. Everything a machine sends is carried across the cell's own network inside another 50 bytes of headers, so a network told to use the wire's own 1500 loses every large packet — which looks like an application bug for a week.

fields.label: VNI
fields.help: The number this cell tags the network's traffic with, so two projects that both use 10.0.0.0/24 never see each other's packets. Left empty, the cell assigns the smallest free one — which is the only correct answer, and not one a tenant can work out.

title: Subnets
blurb: A range on a network, and the count of what IPAM has handed out of it.

fields.label: Network
fields.whenEmpty: No networks in this project yet, and an instance does not need one: left without a network, it joins the project's default, which is made the first time somebody asks. Make one here to lay out the addresses yourself.

fields.label: Resolvers
fields.help: Left empty the instances use this cell's own resolver, which names the project's other machines and forwards everything else. Name one here to send them somewhere of your own instead.

fields.label: Reserved
fields.help: Addresses the platform will not hand out.

title: Ports
blurb: What an instance is attached to the fabric by. Programmed means the agent has it in its maps.

fields.label: Subnet
fields.whenEmpty: No subnets on this network yet. A subnet is the range its addresses come from — make one before a port.

fields.label: Security groups
fields.help: Rules only ever add allowances, so ordering does not matter and two groups cannot contradict each other. With none, the port keeps the platform's default: nothing in, everything out, replies always.

fields.label: Address
fields.help: Left empty IPAM allocates one. It never changes afterwards — an address that moves under a running instance is an outage.

fields.label: Rate limit
fields.help: Zero is unlimited. Multi-tenancy without a ceiling is one noisy neighbour away from an incident.

title: Security groups
blurb: What a port is allowed to carry. Rules only add allowances — ingress is denied, egress is allowed and replies always come back, so a port in no group is not an open one.
empty: No security groups yet. Without one an instance keeps the platform's default — nothing in, everything out, replies always — and a group is how you let something in.

fields.label: Rules
fields.help: Every rule permits; none of them forbids. A group with no rules is a group that allows nothing extra, which is the platform's default anyway: nothing in, everything out, replies always.

title: Image sources
blurb: Where a family's images come from. The cell asks the checksums file what the current digest is, over https so the certificate is checked, and publishes an image when the answer is one it does not have. Nothing about a running instance changes: a machine keeps the bytes it was built from, and "always the newest" means new machines get it.
empty: Nothing is being watched for new builds. A source is a URL and a checksums file; the cell rechecks it and publishes an image whenever the digest it reads has changed.

fields.label: Family
fields.help: Everything this source publishes joins this family, and an instance asking for `families/debian-13` gets the newest of them.

fields.label: Image
fields.help: Where the bytes are. This may be plain http: the digest below is what makes fetching them safe, and a wrong byte gives a wrong digest and fails the fetch.

fields.label: What the bytes are
fields.help: Leave it alone for a `.qcow2` file — the name settles it. Everywhere else it has to be said: nothing here ever fetches the bytes, and the filename lies (Ubuntu ships qcow2 under `.img`). A node handed a mis-declared image refuses the disk, and every instance of this family goes without one.

fields.label: Checksums
fields.help: A `sha256sum`- or `sha512sum`-style file covering the image's filename — Debian publishes only the latter for its cloud images, and either is read. **https only**, and refused otherwise: this is the one value the whole arrangement trusts, and whoever can rewrite it chooses what every new instance in this cell boots.

fields.label: Paused
fields.help: Stop looking, without forgetting where this came from.

fields.label: Check every
fields.help: Six hours when left empty. Cloud images are published daily at best, and a cell that asks every minute spends its day fetching a checksums file to learn nothing.

fields.label: Keep
fields.help: How many of this family to keep. Three when left empty. An image an instance was built from is never taken away, however old — the instance would be unable to start on its next move.

title: Image families
blurb: What to boot, by the name that stays right when the bytes change. A family resolves to the newest image published under it; an instance resolves its family once, when it is made, and keeps the image it got.
empty: Nothing to boot here yet. A family appears as soon as an image this project can see is published carrying one — an image source is the usual way, and publishing an image by hand is the other.

fields.label: Resolves to
fields.help: The image an instance created right now would get.

fields.label: Everybody may boot it
fields.help: Published to the cell rather than kept in one project.

title: Images
blurb: Content-addressed and immutable. Cached copies are a placement preference, never a requirement.
empty: No images yet. An image is one set of bytes under one digest, and an instance built from it keeps those bytes for as long as it lives.

fields.label: Publish from
fields.help: Take the digest, format, size and source from an image that already exists. Nothing is copied — an image is addressed by its digest, so every node that had the bytes still has them. Anything you fill in below wins over what is taken.

fields.label: Family
fields.whenEmpty: Without a family this image can only be asked for by its digest, and nothing will ever offer it as "the newest".
fields.help: What this image is, in the words somebody would use to ask for it. An instance can then name `families/debian-13` and get the newest one there is, resolved when it is created and written down — so an instance never changes its operating system on a restart.

fields.label: Version
fields.help: Which one in the family, for a person to read. Newest is decided by when this cell learned of the image, not by comparing this — every scheme for ordering version strings is wrong for somebody's.

fields.label: Digest
fields.help: The bytes are addressed by this, so an image cannot be replaced under an instance that was built from it.

fields.label: Signature
fields.placeholder: base64 Ed25519 signature over the digest line
fields.help: An Ed25519 signature over the digest line as written — `sha256:<hex>` or `sha512:<hex>` — base64. Accepted only when it verifies under a key the cell was started with; refused otherwise, so a stored signature is a verified one.

fields.label: Life stage

options.label: Deprecated — still boots, no longer chosen
Retired — nothing new is built from it

fields.help: An image is never replaced, only superseded. Deprecating one stops a family choosing it while everything pinned to it keeps working; retiring it refuses anything new. Neither touches a running instance.

fields.label: Use instead
fields.help: Named in the refusal a tenant reads, so they are told where to go rather than only that the door is shut.

fields.label: Shared with
fields.help: Projects that may boot from this image besides this one, or `*` for every project in the cell. A one-way grant: whoever receives it can boot and cannot edit, retire or delete.

title: Migrations
blurb: Moving a running instance to another node. There is no migrating state anywhere: this object is the ask, and whether it is finished is read from where the instance actually runs. Start one from the instance you want to move — the destination is chosen where it is.
empty: Nothing is being moved. A migration is started from the instance you want to move, where the nodes that could take it are known and the rest say why not.

fields.label: From
fields.help: Where it is now. Taken from the instance above.

fields.label: To
fields.help: Only the nodes that can receive this instance can be chosen. The rest are shown with the reason they cannot.

fields.label: Mode
fields.help: What a failure costs. Under Live the instance stays where it is; under Post-copy a failure mid-flight loses it.

fields.label: Downtime budget
fields.help: The pause the instance may take at the end. A busy one needs a larger budget or the transfer never converges.

fields.label: Give up after
fields.help: A migration that cannot converge is one that runs until somebody notices.

fields.label: Streams
fields.help: Parallel streams for the transfer. One is the only value a local socket accepts.

agreements.label: Destination
agreements.note: The node this migration was assigned to is not the one that has reported on it. Nothing is listening for the instance until they agree — the destination has to act first.

title: Nodes
blurb: Hypervisors. The spec is what an operator decided about one; the status is what its agent last reported. Adding one here creates the object and mints its registration token — shown once, because the platform keeps a hash and cannot show it again.
empty: No machines are registered yet. A node is a hypervisor: adding one makes the object and mints the token its agent signs in with, shown once and never again.

fields.label: Accepts work
fields.help: Turning this off drains the node: nothing new is placed, what runs keeps running.

fields.label: Labels
fields.help: What placement policies match on.

fields.label: Move its instances away
fields.help: Separate from draining. Draining says nothing new comes here; this says none of the old stays either. One migration is started per instance that can move — one holding a passed-through device cannot, and stays with the reason on it.

fields.label: Stop its own instances after
fields.help: How long this node may fail to report before it stops the instances it holds. Left empty it never does — and a node that never does is never recovered from, because nothing can tell unreachable from stopped. Set it and instances marked for restart can be brought up elsewhere.

fields.label: Carries external traffic
fields.help: A public address whose network says so is announced from here, and packets for it reach the instance over the overlay. Several machines may carry it — the network above sees them as equal next hops — and a cell with none simply cannot use that mode.

fields.label: vCPUs per core
fields.help: How many vCPUs this machine may hand out per real core. Zero or one means one for one. A processor can be shared — two instances that both want a core get one each in turn, and being wrong costs speed — which is how nearly every fleet in the world is run. There is deliberately no setting for memory: an instance promised 8 GiB and handed 4 is not slow, it is killed.

fields.label: CPU baseline
fields.help: Present the same CPU as other nodes so instances can migrate between them. Those already running keep the CPU they started with and adopt this one when they next restart.

title: Maintenance
blurb: Say in advance that a machine is going out of service, and the cell stops placing work on it when the time comes — without anybody being awake to flip a switch, and without anything to flip back afterwards. Whether a window is upcoming, open or over is read off the clock, so a window that ends puts everything back by ceasing to be open.
empty: No machine is booked out of service. Declare a window and the cell stops placing work on that node when the time comes, and puts it back by itself when the window ends.

fields.label: Node
fields.help: The machine going out of service.

fields.label: Starts
fields.help: In your own timezone. A start already past means now — work that has already begun is a true thing to declare.

fields.label: Lasts
fields.help: How long it stays open. There is no end time to keep in step with this one: two fields that can disagree about the same fact are one field too many.

fields.label: Move the instances off
fields.help: Off — nothing new is placed here and everything already running stays put, which is what a four-minute firmware update wants. On — the instances are migrated away as well, which is what pulling the machine wants. One that cannot move is left where it is, and :explainMaintenance says which.

fields.label: Reason
fields.placeholder: swapping the failed DIMM in slot 3
fields.help: Shown wherever this window is the reason something was refused, so "no capacity" reads as "node-b is out until 03:00 for the memory swap" instead.

title: Snapshot schedules
blurb: The cheap half of the pair. A snapshot lives in the volume's own pool — taken in a moment, costs almost nothing, and lost with the pool it is in. For a copy that survives losing the pool, use a backup schedule.

fields.label: Volume
fields.help: What is snapshotted.

fields.label: Snapshot every
fields.help: Cheap enough to run hourly. A snapshot lives in the volume's own pool: it is the right tool for going back an hour, and it is lost with the pool — which is what backups are for.

fields.label: Keep
fields.help: Only finished ones count, so a run of failures never expires the last one that worked. Snapshots taken by hand are never expired.

title: Captures
blurb: Build an instance by hand, get it right, capture it — then every instance made from the result starts where that one left off. It has to be stopped first: a disk copied from under a running machine is crash-consistent, and a template is stamped out by people who assume it is clean.

fields.label: Instance
fields.help: It must be stopped. A disk copied from under a running machine is crash-consistent, which a template stamped out a hundred times must not be — if you want a copy of a running instance, take a backup instead.

fields.label: Name it
fields.help: What the resulting image is called. Its digest is added to this — a list of hashes is not something anybody chooses from.

fields.label: Keep it on
fields.help: Where the bytes go. Any node that can reach the same path can then boot instances from the image.

title: Backup targets
blurb: Where backups are kept. Deliberately not a pool: a copy that lives beside the original is a snapshot, and is lost with the pool it is in. A target in a volume's own pool is refused.
empty: Nowhere to put backups yet. A target is a path the cell can write copies to, somewhere other than the pool holding the volume — a copy beside the original is lost with it.

fields.label: Path
fields.help: An absolute path the agent can already write to. Mounting an NFS or CIFS share is the host's job, not this platform's — one that managed its own mounts would be a second, worse copy of what init already does.

fields.label: Accepts backups
fields.help: Turning this off stops new copies going here. What is already here stays, and can still be restored from.

fields.label: Reported on by
fields.help: The pool agent that says whether this path is there, whether it can be written, and how much room is left. Named rather than claimed by whoever gets there first — a target assigned to nobody is one any agent could report on. Leave it empty and nobody looks: copies are still written by the pool holding the volume, and a path it cannot reach fails on the backup instead.

fields.label: Read a copy back every
fields.help: How often a copy here is read back and checked against what it hashed to when it was written. 0 never checks, which is the default: verification reads every byte of a copy, and that is real I/O somebody has to decide to spend. Without it, 'the backup exists' is the only thing anybody can say about it. One copy per pass, the one whose last check is stalest — so a target holding more copies checks each of them less often rather than falling behind on the work that is not optional.

title: Backups
blurb: One copy of one volume, at one moment. Restoring makes a new volume from a copy — never writing one back over the original, which would be a command living in a spec and carried out again on every resync.
empty: No copies of anything yet. A backup is one volume at one moment, kept off the pool it lives on; restoring one makes a new volume rather than writing over the old.

fields.label: Volume
fields.help: What is copied.

fields.label: Target
fields.help: Where the copy goes. Left empty, the cell's most roomy accepting target answers. A target in the volume's own pool is refused: a copy beside the original is a snapshot, and is lost with the pool it is in.

title: Backup schedules
blurb: An intention, not a job queue: there should be a copy of this volume no older than the interval, and the last few kept. What exists is what decides — a copy still being made holds the schedule, and a stuck one holds it for one interval and no longer.

fields.label: Volume
fields.help: What is copied.

fields.label: Target
fields.help: Where the copies go.

fields.label: Copy every
fields.help: How stale the newest copy may get before another is made. An interval rather than a cron line, because the only question anybody asks a schedule is when it will next run.

fields.label: Keep
fields.help: How many of this schedule's copies to keep. Only finished copies count, so a run of failures never expires the last one that worked. Copies taken by hand are never expired.

title: Audit
blurb: What was refused, and who signed in. Not a log of everything that happened — every successful write already leaves an operation carrying its target, its verb and who asked. What no operation exists for is a request that was turned down, and that is the one a multi-tenant cell gets asked about later.
empty: No records yet. This is where a refusal and a sign-in are kept; a change that went through is not here, it left an operation instead.

title: Device classes
blurb: Names for interchangeable hardware. An instance asks for a class, never an address: an address belongs to one machine, so an instance naming one could only ever run there. A device is offered only when everything in its IOMMU group is free — a group is passed through whole or not at all.
empty: No hardware is offered for passing through. A class names the cards that are interchangeable, so an instance can ask for one without naming the machine it is in.

fields.label: PCI ids
fields.help: vendor:device, as `lspci -n` prints it. Several, because a fleet buys the same accelerator across board revisions.

fields.label: Description
fields.help: What to call it in this console.

title: Flavors
blurb: Named machine sizes, offered by the cell. An instance is an m1-small, not a hand-entered triple of numbers — the sizes that land on the fleet are the shapes it was bought for. Whether a project may also size by hand is that project's policy.
empty: This cell offers no named sizes, so every instance has to be sized by hand — and every project needs the cell's leave to do that.

fields.label: Description
fields.help: One sentence for the picker. The numbers already say most of it.

title: BGP peers
blurb: Sessions from the cell's gateways to the routers in front of it. What gets announced is derived, never listed: every external subnet, and a host route for each public address that is in front of something — so the router ahead of the cell and this console cannot disagree about what the cell claims.
empty: No sessions to the routers in front of this cell. Until one comes up the cell announces nothing, and a public address an instance holds is unreachable from outside.

fields.label: Peer address
fields.help: The router or firewall in front of the cell.

fields.label: Speaks from
fields.help: The machine that holds the session — a gateway, with FRR installed. One session is one speaker.

fields.label: TCP-MD5 password
fields.help: The same string the router has for this session (RFC 2385). Most firewalls will not bring a session up without one.

fields.label: Hops to the peer
fields.help: Only when the router is not on the same wire: eBGP refuses a neighbour more than one hop away unless told the distance.

title: Routers
blurb: Which of this project's networks reach each other. A membership rather than a box: there is nothing to place and nothing to fail over — the gateway answers on whichever machine the packet is already on. The routed VNI and gateway MAC are what the cell tags and addresses that traffic with; nothing inside a machine has to know either.
empty: This project's networks do not reach each other. A router is a membership: list the networks that should be able to talk and the platform routes between them.

fields.label: Networks
fields.help: The networks whose subnets reach each other. A network belongs to at most one router.

title: Floating IPs
blurb: Addresses that outlive the machine answering on them. The address is held by the declaration, not by the port, so replacing an instance does not change what the outside world reaches.
empty: No public addresses yet. A floating IP is held by the project rather than by the machine, so the address survives the instance behind it being replaced.

fields.label: Instance
fields.whenEmpty: This project has no instances yet; a public address goes in front of one.
fields.help: The instance this address sits in front of. Its interface and the cell's public pool are found for you — name the subnet under More settings to choose v6, or a particular pool.

fields.label: Subnet
fields.help: Where the address comes from. Left empty, the cell's public pool answers — IPv4 first. Naming a subnet is how you choose v6, or a particular pool.

fields.label: Address
fields.help: Leave empty to be given the lowest address nothing else holds.

fields.label: Forwards to
fields.help: The port this address reaches. Clearing it holds the address while the machine behind it is replaced.

fields.label: The instance
fields.help: Held by the instance means the address is bound to its port and configured inside the machine — nothing rewrites a packet, and the machine can tell anybody its own address, which SIP, FTP, IPsec and mDNS all need. Translated means the edge answers for it and the machine never knows. A held address has to come from an external network.

fields.label: Announced by
fields.help: The machine holding the instance is the shortest path: nothing is encapsulated for traffic to and from the world, and the route follows a live migration by itself. It needs every hypervisor to be allowed to peer with the router above it. A gateway node needs only that one machine to peer, and costs a detour in both directions.

title: Load balancers
blurb: One address in front of many ports. The network itself balances by connection, on whichever machine the traffic arrives at — there is no appliance to place and nothing to fail over. Nothing here probes a member's health: the pool is what was declared, not a judgement about it.
empty: No load balancers yet. One address in front of many instances, spread by connection — there is no appliance to place and nothing to fail over.

fields.label: Network
fields.help: The network the address lives on. It scopes the service, so two projects may front the same address on different networks.

fields.label: Subnet
fields.help: Where the address comes from. The same counting as a port's address and a floating IP's, so no two of them are ever the same address.

fields.label: Listeners
fields.help: The ports the address answers on. Traffic is spread across the pool by connection, so one client's connection stays on one member.

fields.label: Members
fields.help: The ports behind the address — ports, not addresses, so an instance that moves stays in the pool. Empty holds the address and forwards to nothing.

fields.label: Address
fields.help: Leave empty to be given the lowest address nothing else holds.

fields.label: Keep a client on one member
fields.help: For a service that keeps something per client between connections — a session in memory, an upload in pieces. The cost: one client is one member, so a pool fronting few busy clients spreads worse, and everyone behind one NAT counts as one client.

fields.label: Draining
fields.help: Members being taken out of service: they take no new connections and keep the ones they have until the clients are done. Every name here has to be one of the members. Removing a member outright cuts its connections instead.

agreements.label: Address
agreements.note: The address asked for is not the one the network serves yet. Usually the world catching up; if it stays, the Ready condition says what is in the way.

title: Pools
blurb: Where volumes live. The spec is what an operator decided about a pool; the backend, the capacity and what is used are what its agent found.
empty: No storage has been declared. A pool is where volumes live: the object is made here and the agent that claims it reports the backend, the capacity and what is used.

fields.label: On one machine
fields.help: The machine this pool's bytes are on, where that is one machine. Leave it empty for storage every node can reach — a Ceph pool, an NFS mount — which is what the platform assumes when nothing is said. A directory or an LVM group is on one host, and until the object said so the platform would put a volume there, schedule the guest that needs it somewhere else, and let the attach fail with a path the tenant cannot act on.

fields.label: Accepts new volumes
fields.help: Turning this off drains the pool: nothing new is provisioned into it, what it holds stays.

fields.label: Labels
fields.help: What a volume's placement matches on.

fields.label: Ceiling — IOPS
fields.help: The most any one volume in this pool may take. A volume that names nothing of its own gets this; one that asks for more is brought down to it. Left empty there is no ceiling.

title: Usage
blurb: What this project had, read once an hour and kept for ninety days. A reading is a sample, not a total: something created and destroyed between two of them is in neither. Quota says what is in use now; this is the only thing that remembers.
empty: Nothing has been read yet. A reading is taken once an hour, so a project made within the hour has none; ninety days of them are kept after that.

title: Operations
blurb: Something that could not finish inside a request. Finished is computed from the target itself — whether the object has caught up with what was asked of it — so an operation cannot disagree with the thing it describes.

fields.label: Waiting for generation
fields.help: Which version of the target's spec this was asked against. The operation is finished when the target reports having caught up with that version — which is why it cannot disagree with the object it describes.

title: Users
blurb: Who can sign in. A password is set from the row rather than shown on it — the platform stores a hash and cannot recover the original, which is the point.

fields.label: Service account
fields.help: A program rather than a person: it signs in with no password and carries a token instead, minted by an operator and shown once. It is named in a project's bindings like anybody else and gets the same four roles.

fields.label: Display name
fields.help: Shown on screen. Never used to decide anything — the account's id is its identity.

fields.label: Disabled
fields.help: Ends every session this account holds immediately, and refuses new sign-ins. Its roles are kept, so turning it back on restores exactly what it had.

fields.label: Cell administrator
fields.help: May do anything anywhere in this cell, including inside every project. Grant it to operate the platform, not to use it.

title: Ceph
blurb: Cluster storage every node reaches, instead of a pool per machine. Optional: a cell with directory pools is a working cell, and nothing here turns itself on. Choosing a disk for an OSD erases it.
empty: No Ceph cluster here. A cell runs at most one, and only where every node should reach the same storage — a pool on each machine is a working cell without it.

fields.label: Network
fields.help: Where the daemons talk to each other and to clients. A node with several interfaces has several answers, and the wrong one puts replication traffic on the tenant network.

fields.label: Replication network
fields.help: A separate network for replication. Empty means the one above carries both, which is the ordinary answer for a small cluster.

fields.label: Monitors
fields.help: Three nodes, or one for a lab. Never two: a quorum of two survives no failures and looks like it would.

fields.label: Disks

refusals.text: it has a partition table with {partitions} partition(s) on it. Something laid this disk out deliberately; wipe it outside the platform if it really is spare.
it holds a {fstype} filesystem. Handing it to Ceph erases that, so it is not offered until the filesystem is gone.
it is mounted at {at} right now. Whatever is using it is using it.
it holds swap or the root filesystem — consuming it takes this node down.
it is a member of {of}. Take it out of that first, if that is really what you want.

fields.tooSmall: it is {sizeGib} GiB, and an OSD wants at least {minGib}. Below that the OSD's own bookkeeping is a meaningful fraction of the disk.
fields.unknown: this node reports it as {kind}, which this console has no answer for. Not offered: a disk whose state cannot be read is not a disk anything here can call empty.
fields.warning: Adding a disk here erases it. Everything on that device goes, and nothing in this platform brings it back.
fields.help: One disk, one OSD. Anything that cannot be chosen says why beside it rather than being greyed out — only a device the node can see is empty is offered, so a disk you really do want to give up has to be wiped outside the platform first.

fields.label: Pools
fields.help: Where volumes are stored. Copies is how many of every object exist; below the floor the pool refuses writes rather than holding data it cannot protect — so a floor equal to the copies means one node rebooting stops writing.

fields.label: Paused
fields.help: Stops the deployment where it stands. Nothing is torn down, and turning it off carries on from there.

agreements.label: Monitors
agreements.note: A monitor that was chosen is not running. Until the quorum is what was asked for, the cluster tolerates fewer failures than it looks like it does.

title: Roles
blurb: The four rungs say how much somebody may do. A role here says *what* — collection by collection, for the case a rung cannot express: may restart the database machines, may not touch the network.
empty: No roles of your own. The four rungs cover most of what anybody grants; one of these is worth making when a rung says more, or less, than you mean.

fields.label: What it is for
fields.placeholder: Restart the database machines, nothing else
fields.help: Somebody granting this will read this line and nothing else.

fields.label: Grants
fields.help: A verb, and the collections it applies to. Being able to act on something carries being able to see it — anything else is a button that works above a screen that shows nothing.

title: Folders
blurb: A place to put projects, and a place to grant a role once instead of forty times. Roles granted here reach everything below.
empty: No folders yet. A folder holds projects so that a role can be granted once above them instead of once on each.

fields.label: Inside
fields.whenEmpty: There are no folders yet. The first one goes at the top.
fields.help: Left empty this folder sits at the top. Roles granted above it reach in here too.

title: Projects
blurb: The quota and access anchor. Usage is counted from what exists, never decremented by hand.
empty: No projects yet. Everything that costs anything — instances, volumes, addresses — lives in one, and quota and access are set on it.

fields.label: Host bridges this project may use
fields.help: One bridge per line, as they are named on the nodes. A network put on one takes its instances off this platform's networks and onto whatever the machine is on — no address from us, no gateway, no security group. Empty means this project gets logical networks only, which is what a new customer should have. Named rather than a yes/no, because what anybody means by a host bridge is a particular wire.

fields.label: May pass hardware through
fields.help: Whether instances here may be given a GPU or a NIC of their own. A passed-through device is a physical thing one instance holds and no other can have, so a project that may ask for them can empty a node of the hardware everybody else was scheduled against.

fields.label: May hold public addresses
fields.help: Whether this project may claim addresses the world can reach. They come out of address space the cell was given by whoever is above it, so a project that could mint them could exhaust the pool every other project is waiting on.

fields.label: May size instances by hand
fields.help: Whether instances here may be sized by typed numbers instead of a flavor. Only asked once the cell has flavors at all: with a menu defined, the closed answer is the sold one, and this is the deliberate exception for the customer whose shapes are their own.

fields.label: Folder
fields.help: Roles granted on the folder reach every project under it. Quota and policy are this project's own.

fields.label: Cell
fields.help: A cell is one installation of this platform — its own machines, its own network and its own address space, administered as one thing. This says which of them holds this project's resources and where requests for them are routed. Leave empty to use whichever cell answers, which is what an installation with one cell wants.

fields.label: Instances
fields.help: How many instances may exist here at once, running or not. Left empty there is no limit — an empty box is stored as a zero, and the platform reads a zero quota as no cap rather than as none allowed.

fields.label: vCPUs
fields.help: Counted across every instance that exists, whether or not it is running. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Memory
fields.help: Counted across every instance that exists, whether or not it is running. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Volume space
fields.help: The sizes of this project's volumes added up. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Volumes
fields.help: A count, separate from the space: per-volume overhead is a different worry from capacity, and the two are capped apart. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Floating IPs
fields.help: An address that outlives the machine answering on it is scarce and externally routable. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Load balancers
fields.help: Each one takes an address out of a subnet and an entry on every host that traffic arrives at. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Passed-through devices
fields.help: Each one is a piece of hardware that exists once and cannot be oversubscribed, so without a cap one project can take every accelerator in the cell. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Snapshots
fields.help: Cheap to ask for and occupying a pool for as long as they exist. A schedule nobody is watching is the ordinary way a cell fills up. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Snapshot storage
fields.help: Counted from what each snapshot turned out to occupy, which the pool reports after the fact. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Backups
fields.help: Separate from snapshots because they live on a backup target rather than in the pool. Left empty there is no limit.

fields.label: Backup storage
fields.help: Counted from what each backup turned out to occupy. Left empty there is no limit.
